title: Electrical Engineering Simply Explained
fullText: Struggling with math? Check out the Math Bundle. Five complete guides covering calculus, algebra, trigonometry, geometry, and statistics. No fluff, just clear explanations that actually make sense. Everything's laid out for you. Grab all five books in one place. Um, and if you're on your phone right now, just scan the QR code on screen to go straight to the site. Links are also in the description and comment section. Join hundreds of viewers who've already grabbed it. And now, let's get into it. You sat through a class where you memorized Ohm's law, drew circuit diagrams on paper, and calculated voltage drops well enough to pass a test. Then you closed the notebook and never actually understood what electricity is or what it does. That gap has probably followed you every time you've stared at a breaker panel or wondered why one charger fried your phone and another one didn't. This video closes that gap, not with more formulas to memorize, but with the actual understanding of what is happening inside the wires around you every day. Electrical engineering exists because electricity is a form of usable energy that you cannot see, and it is dangerous if left uncontrolled. Long before anyone built a power grid, people needed a systematic way to move energy from where it is generated to where it is needed and to do it safely and predictably. That is the real problem. This field solves a power plant makes electricity. A lamp, a motor or a laptop uses it. Everything in between exists to get that energy from the source to the task without anyone getting hurt and without the energy being wasted. Every single concept you are about to learn serves one of three purposes. Generating electricity, moving it somewhere, or converting it into useful work. Let's start with voltage. Voltage is the push behind electric charge. It is the difference in electrical potential between two points that makes charge want to move from one point to the other. Voltage exists because nothing in a circuit moves on its own. There has to be a difference, a kind of imbalance for current to flow at all. This matters because it explains why some electrical sources feel harmless and others do not. A car battery is rated at 12 Vts. You can touch both terminals with bare hands and feel nothing dangerous. A household outlet in the United States is rated at 120 volts and in many other countries at 240 volts. Touch the exposed contacts of that outlet and the result can be lethal. Every voltage source, whether it's a battery, a wall outlet, or a power line running down your street, is doing the exact same job at different scales. It is maintaining a difference in potential that will push charge through anything connected between its two points, including a human body. If that connection happens to form, the key point is that voltage is the pressure driving electricity and higher voltage means a stronger push behind the charge trying to move through you. Current is the next piece. Current is the actual rate at which charge flows through a conductor measured in amps. This matters because current, not voltage, is what does the work and what causes damage. A high voltage source with almost no current available can be far less dangerous than a lower voltage source that can deliver a lot of current. Here's what's actually happening when you plug the wrong charger into your phone. Every charger is rated for a certain amperage. If you use a charger built to deliver more current than your phone's battery and circuitry are designed to handle, the excess current shows up as heat inside the device. Over time or all at once, that heat degrades the battery or damages the internal circuitry. This is also why thick cables are used for high current applications like welding equipment or an electric vehicle charger. While a thin wire works fine for something like a phone charger that only needs to move a small current. The thickness of a conductor directly affects how much current it can carry without overheating. The key point is that current is the actual flow doing the work. And matching the rated amperage of a device matters just as much as matching its voltage. Resistance is what a material does when it opposes the flow of current. No material conducts electricity perfectly. Copper wire is an excellent conductor, but it still has some resistance, and that resistance turns a small amount of electrical energy into heat as current passes through it. This matters because resistance is not just a nuisance number in an equation. It is the reason wires can overheat. Think about a frayed or damaged extension cord. One where the copper strands inside have been cut or crushed in one section. That damaged section has less material to carry the same current. So its resistance increases at that exact point. All the heat that would normally spread evenly across the whole length of wire now concentrates in that one weak spot. And that is how extension cords catch fire. This same principle explains why some materials are chosen specifically for their high resistance. The heating element inside a toaster or a space heater is made from a material with deliberately high resistance because in that case the goal is to generate heat on purpose rather than avoid it. The key point is that resistance turns electrical energy into heat and damaged wiring concentrates that heat in one dangerous location instead of spreading it safely. Now those three ideas connect through Ohm's law. Ohm's law states that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance. This matters because it lets engineers predict exactly how a circuit will behave before they ever build it. If you know two of the three values, you can calculate the third. This is the important part because this single relationship is what allows an electrician to size a circuit breaker correctly for a home. If they know the voltage supplied and the expected resistance of the wiring and devices on that circuit, they can calculate how much current will flow and they choose a breaker rated to shut off power before that current gets high enough to overheat the wires. The key point is that Ohm's law is not an abstract formula. It is the calculation that keeps your home's wiring from becoming a fire hazard. Circuits are the actual paths that current travels along and how components are connected changes how the whole system behaves. In a series circuit, everything is connected along a single path one after another. In a parallel circuit, components are connected along separate branches that all draw from the same source. Here is why this matters in practice. Old style holiday lights were wired in series. So if one bulb burned out, it broke the entire path and the whole string went dark. Modern LED holiday lights are wired in parallel. So each bulb has its own independent path back to the source. And one burned out bulb has no effect on the rest of the string. The key point is that the way components are wired together, not just what the components are, determines how a failure in one part affects the whole system. Power is the rate at which energy is used or delivered and it is calculated as voltage multiplied by current. This matters because power measured in watts is exactly what your electric bill charges you for. It is also what determines how much heat and demand a device places on a circuit. Compare a 1500 W space heater to a 60W light bulb plugged into the same outlet. The space heater draws far more current at the same voltage, which is why running it alongside other hydraw appliances on one circuit can trip a breaker, while the light bulb could run for hours without ever coming close to that limit. This is also why appliance labels list wattage instead of just current. Wattage gives you the full picture of demand in a single number, combining both the voltage supplied and the current the device draws. A homeowner adding up the wattage of everything plugged into one circuit, a microwave, a coffee maker, and a toaster running at the same time, can predict whether that circuit is about to trip before it actually happens. The key point is that wattage tells you the real demand a device places on your electrical system. And that demand is what circuits and breakers are built to handle safely. Electricity also comes in two forms, alternating current and direct current. Alternating current or AC is electricity that reverses direction periodically. Direct current or DC flows in one direction only. Both exist because each is better suited to a different job. AC is what your power company sends to your home because it can be transmitted over long distances with far less energy loss than DC. Most electronics, on the other hand, actually run on DC internally. Now, here's why this matters to you. That bulky brick built into your laptop charger is not just a plug. It contains a converter that takes the AC power from your wall outlet and transforms it into the steady DC power your laptop's battery and circuits actually need. Without that conversion step, plugging your laptop directly into a wall outlet would destroy it instantly. This same conversion is happening inside a car as well, just in the opposite direction. A car's alternator actually generates alternating current while the engine runs, but the car's battery and most of its electrical systems run on direct current. So, the alternator includes a built-in converter that changes that AC into DC before it ever reaches the battery. The key point is that the electricity in your walls and the electricity your devices run on are not the same thing and that brick is doing real work every time you charge something. The last core concept is grounding. Grounding provides a safe path for excess or stray current to travel into the earth instead of through a person's body. It exists specifically as a protection mechanism against electrical faults. This matters because without it, a malfunctioning appliance or a damaged wire inside a wall could send current through anyone who happens to touch it. This is why a three-prongong outlet is safer than an older two-prong outlet. The third prong connects to a dedicated ground path. So if a fault occurs inside a device, the excess current has a safe route to follow instead of passing through whoever is holding it. This is also why appliances with a metal casing, like a washing machine or a power drill, are required to have a grounded plug. If a wire inside ever comes loose and touches that metal casing, the ground path carries the current away safely instead of leaving the entire casing electrically charged and waiting for someone to touch it. The key point is that grounding is not decoration on a plug. It is an active safety system working every time you use a properly wired outlet. Let me show you exactly how this works when all of these ideas come together in a real situation. Picture a homeowner adding a window air conditioning unit to an older bedroom that only has one outlet on a shared circuit. The circuit is rated at 120 volts. The new AC unit has a specific amperage rating printed on its label, and that current draw adds to whatever else is already running on that same circuit. The wire running to that outlet has a fixed gauge, which determines its resistance and how much current it can safely carry before overheating. Using power equals voltage multiplied by current, an electrician can calculate the total wattage demand of everything on that circuit at once. If the combined current draw exceeds what the wire gauge and the breaker are rated to handle safely, the breaker will trip or worse, the wire could overheat before the breaker reacts. This is exactly why an electrician calculates total amperage on a circuit before approving a new appliance installation. Skipping that step is how homeowners end up with breakers that trip constantly or in worst cases wiring that overheats inside the wall where nobody can see it happening. A few mistakes come up constantly and they are easy to make because the language around electricity gets used loosely in everyday conversation. People often treat voltage and current as if they are the same thing, assuming that anything labeled high voltage is automatically more dangerous. The fix is remembering that current is what actually causes harm and voltage is simply the force driving that current. So the real danger depends on both together. Another common mistake is assuming that any device is safe to plug in as long as it physically fits the outlet without considering its wattage relative to what else is running on that circuit. The fix is checking the total load, not just whether the plug matches the socket. People also tend to think of AC and DC as just two arbitrary types of electricity rather than understanding why each one is used where it is. The fix is connecting the choice directly to the job. AC for long-d distanceance transmission and DC for most electronic components. Finally, many people treat grounding as a building code technicality rather than an active safety feature, which is easy to do since you never see it working under normal conditions. The fix is understanding that grounding only becomes visible in its job the moment something goes wrong and that is exactly when you need it working correctly. This understanding pays off in specific situations. Choosing the correct gauge extension cord for a power tool matters because the wrong gauge risks overheating and fire, especially on long runs or highdraw tools. Understanding your home's breaker panel well enough to know why a specific circuit keeps tripping can save you an unnecessary electrician visit. Or it can stop you from ignoring a real hazard by simply resetting the breaker over and over. Reading the voltage and amperage label on a charger or adapter before buying one prevents damaging expensive electronics with a mismatched power source. Recognizing where GFCI outlets are required in kitchens, bathrooms, and outdoor spaces prevents a dangerous shock in exactly the locations where water and electricity are most likely to meet. You can now look at any electrical spec label and understand exactly what it is telling you. You can explain why a breaker trips instead of just resetting it and hoping it does not happen again. You can evaluate whether an outlet or a circuit can safely handle a new device before you ever plug it in. You are no longer working from memorized formulas. You now have the actual working model that electrical engineers use to think through these problems. And that is the understanding you should have walked away with the first time you sat through this material. Before you go, do like hundreds of others and make sure to grab the math bundle.
